periods.activity_title: Grids Across History: Why Coordinates Were Invented

time_bands.activity: Open with a quick discussion: ask students how they would direct a friend to a specific seat in a large cinema hall with numbered rows and columns. Collect two or three responses, then note that this everyday act is precisely what a coordinate system formalises. Establish the chapter's central question: how can any location on a flat surface be named unambiguously with numbers?

Walk students through the historical narrative in Section 1.1: grid-based thinking in Bharat, transmission through Arabic scholarship into European mathematics, and the key insight that Brahmagupta's formalisation of zero and negative numbers is the necessary precondition for a four-quadrant plane. Students annotate a simple timeline sketch in their notebooks, noting each cultural contribution. Invite conjectures: what happens to the coordinate system if negative numbers are not available?

Pair discussion: students write two sentences explaining, in their own words, why a number system without negatives can only describe one quarter of an infinite flat plane. Pairs share with the class; the teacher collects the key ideas on the board — particularly that only one quadrant is accessible without signed numbers.

Consolidation: students individually write one sentence connecting Brahmagupta's work to what they expect to encounter later in the chapter. Teacher reads two or three responses aloud to close the unit on the chapter's historical grounding.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit sets up the intellectual motivation for the entire chapter by grounding coordinates in a continuous historical narrative rather than jumping to definitions. A common point of confusion is treating the history as decorative: guide students to see that the four-quadrant plane is literally impossible without signed arithmetic, so the history is structural. End-of-Chapter Q5 (p.12) would make a good self-study read after this unit.

periods.activity_title: Reiaan's Room: Informal Grid Representation of a Real Space
materials: Graph paper or squared-paper sheets (one per student)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of Reiaan's room grid (Section 1.2)

textbook_items_in_class.description: For a city grid of 10 streets in each of the N-S and E-W directions spaced 200 m apart, draw a 1 cm = 200 m model and, using the (N-S street, E-W street) intersection convention, find how many intersections can be labelled (4,3) and how many can be labelled (3,4).

time_bands.activity: Read aloud the opening of Section 1.2: Reiaan and Shalini use pins and thread on a rectangular grid to represent the layout of a real room. Ask students: before any axes or coordinates are introduced, what information does a scaled grid already give you? Collect responses; establish that scale and relative position are already present in a grid, even before signed numbers appear.

Students reproduce Reiaan's room grid on their own squared paper at the same 1 cm : 1 ft scale described in Section 1.2, marking the corners and a door position as shown in the textbook figure. The task is deliberate scale practice: every student places at least three key points and labels them informally (no coordinates yet). Circulate and prompt: 'How far is this point from the left wall? From the bottom wall?'

Introduce End of Chapter Q14 (p.13) as a parallel real-world application of the same grid idea: a city block with 10 N-S and 10 E-W streets spaced 200 m apart. Students draw the 1 cm = 200 m model on their paper and work through the question of how many intersections can carry the label (4,3) and how many can carry (3,4). The question's purpose here is to expose the ambiguity that arises without an agreed ordered-pair convention.

Class discussion: students share their answers for how many intersections can be labelled (4,3) versus (3,4). Guide them to articulate that only one intersection per label exists once the convention is fixed — this is the unit's closing insight. Teacher notes the distinction between a grid (which has position) and a coordinate system (which also has signed convention and a fixed origin).

periods.teacher_notes: The informal grid phase is essential: students who jump straight to (x,y) notation often carry the misconception that coordinates are just 'the numbers on the axes' rather than perpendicular distances from a fixed origin. Watch for students labelling points by counting grid squares from the corner rather than from a fixed reference — this is not an error here, but it previews the ambiguity that the formal system resolves. End of Chapter Q14 (p.13) part (i) is accessible to all students at this stage; the ordering ambiguity in part (ii) is the productive struggle to leave open.

periods.activity_title: Axes, Origin, Quadrants, and the Sign Convention
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure showing the x-axis, y-axis, origin, and four quadrants (Section 1.3)

textbook_items_in_class.description: State the x-coordinate and y-coordinate of the point of intersection of the two axes.
Given point W with x-coordinate -5, predict the coordinates of point H on the line through W parallel to the y-axis, and state which quadrants H can lie in.

time_bands.activity: Formally define, on the board, the x-axis and y-axis as two perpendicular lines, the origin O as their intersection with coordinates (0,0), and the sign convention: right and above are positive, left and below are negative. Define the four quadrants by their sign patterns (I: +,+; II: −,+; III: −,−; IV: +,−). Students copy the diagram into their notebooks and annotate each quadrant's sign pair.

Explain that a point on the x-axis takes the form (x, 0) and a point on the y-axis takes the form (0, y), and that for any point in the plane the x-coordinate is its perpendicular distance from the y-axis (signed) and the y-coordinate its perpendicular distance from the x-axis (signed). Work through End of Chapter Q1 (p.12) as a class: what are the coordinates of the intersection of the two axes? Students answer individually first, then discuss. Then tackle End of Chapter Q2 (p.12): given W with x-coordinate −5, what form must H take, and in which quadrants can it lie? Students justify in writing.

Think-and-Reflect from Section 1.3 (first prompt): must a point on an axis always have a zero coordinate? Students reason individually, then discuss in pairs. Bring out the deductive argument: if a point is on the x-axis, it has zero perpendicular distance from the x-axis, so its y-coordinate is 0 by definition — not by convention but by the meaning of 'coordinate'. Then pose the second prompt: does swapping a point's coordinates ever yield the same point? Students conjecture and test with examples.

Quick individual check: each student marks three points on a rough sketch of the plane — one in each of two different quadrants and one on an axis — and states the sign of each coordinate with a one-phrase justification. Teacher circulates and addresses the common sign-confusion at the border of quadrants II and III.

periods.teacher_notes: The most persistent error at this stage is confusing which axis a coordinate measures distance from: students routinely write 'the x-coordinate tells you how far from the x-axis', reversing the definition. Make the deductive chain explicit: the x-coordinate is the perpendicular distance from the y-axis because it measures horizontal displacement. The Think-and-Reflect question about swapping coordinates is worth pressing — swapping (a, b) gives the same point only when a = b, which many students discover by algebra rather than by geometry.

periods.activity_title: Locating Doors and Furniture: Applying Coordinates to Reiaan's Room
periods.visual_aids: Fig. 1.3 from the textbook (Reiaan's room with corners O, A, B, C and doors marked)

textbook_items_in_class.description: Using Fig. 1.3 (Reiaan's room with corners O, A, B, C marked on the axes), find the distance of the door D1R1 from the y-axis and x-axis, state the coordinates of D1, find the door's width given R1 = (11.5, 0), and compare the bathroom door width (B1 (0,1.5) to B2 (0,4)) with the room door's width.

Given three feet of a rectangular study table at (8,9), (11,9), (11,7), find the fourth foot's coordinates, judge whether the spot is suitable, and state the table's width and length from the coordinates.
Given the bathroom door hinge at B1 opening into the bedroom, determine whether it would hit the wardrobe and suggest changes if the door were made wider.

time_bands.activity: Students open to Fig. 1.3 and Exercise Set 1.1 (p.5). Brief orientation: the room corners lie on the axes, so their coordinates take the axis forms established in the previous unit (x, 0) or (0, y). Ask students to locate corner A on their figure and state its coordinates before any computation begins.

Students work through Exercise Set 1.1 (i)-(iv) (p.5) individually. The key moves are: reading the perpendicular distance of D1 from each axis directly from the figure, writing its coordinates, and then computing the door width as a coordinate difference along the x-axis. Circulate; the comparison of door widths in part (iv) requires reading two y-axis intercepts and taking the difference — prompt students to see this as a distance along the y-axis.

Students work Exercise Set 1.2 Q1 (p.8) — finding the fourth foot of the study table given three feet — and Q2 (p.8) — the bathroom door clearance question. For Q1, the key insight is that opposite vertices of a rectangle share exactly one coordinate; students who list all four pairs and check are more reliable than those who guess. For Q2, the spatial reasoning (will the door arc hit the wardrobe?) is done by interpreting coordinates as distances.

Whole-class debrief: one student presents the fourth-foot coordinates for Q1 with justification, and one presents the door-clearance reasoning for Q2. Teacher resolves any disagreements by referring back to the definition of a rectangle's opposite vertices sharing one coordinate — the deductive anchor for the answer.

periods.teacher_notes: Exercise Set 1.1 (p.5) part (iv) trips students who subtract in the wrong order and get a negative door width — remind them that width is a distance (always positive) and should be computed as the larger coordinate minus the smaller. For Exercise Set 1.2 Q1 (p.8), the error to watch is placing the fourth foot by visual symmetry rather than by the algebraic property of a rectangle's shared coordinates; ask those students to justify why their answer is correct.
homework: Complete Exercise Set 1.2 Q3 and Q4 (p.8): state corner coordinates for the bathroom and place the dining-room table at the room's centre with corner coordinates.

periods.activity_title: Coordinate Reasoning: Quadrilateral RAMP and a City Grid

textbook_items_in_class.description: Given R(3,0), A(0,-2), M(-5,-2), P(-5,2) joined in order as quadrilateral RAMP, predict two perpendicular sides, one side parallel to an axis, and two points that are mirror images of each other in an axis; then plot and verify.
Discuss what a coordinate system would be like without negative numbers, and whether such a system could locate all points on a 2-D plane.

time_bands.activity: Warm up by asking students to state, from the sign-convention rules, which quadrant each of R(3,0), A(0,−2), M(−5,−2), P(−5,2) lies in or on. Students answer individually. The point R is on the x-axis and A on the y-axis — confirm that axis points belong to no quadrant, which reinforces the sign-pattern definition established earlier.

Students plot R, A, M, P on graph paper and join them in order to form quadrilateral RAMP. They then answer End of Chapter Q3 (p.12) parts by parts: (i) identify two perpendicular sides by examining whether the sides are horizontal, vertical, or neither; (ii) identify one side parallel to an axis; (iii) identify two points that are mirror images in an axis — M(−5,−2) and P(−5,2) are reflections in the x-axis. Students write a one-sentence justification for each claim before the class discussion.

Short written task using End of Chapter Q5 (p.12): in three to four sentences students argue whether a coordinate system without negative numbers could locate all points on a flat plane. The expected argument draws on the sign convention — without negatives, only Quadrant I is accessible, so points left of or below O cannot be named. Two students read their arguments; the class checks for completeness.

Consolidation: teacher draws a quick blank coordinate grid on the board and places two points, one in Quadrant II and one in Quadrant IV, asking students to name each and state what would happen to these names in a system with only non-negative numbers. This closes the unit on the consequences of the sign convention.

periods.teacher_notes: End of Chapter Q3 (p.12) part (iii) — identifying mirror images — reaches into the reflection idea that Section 1.4 develops fully; treat it here as a coordinate-reading observation (M and P share the same x-coordinate and have y-coordinates that are negatives of each other) rather than as a proof about reflections. A common slip in plotting RAMP is placing R at (0,3) instead of (3,0); watch for axis-transposition errors and use them as teaching moments about the ordered-pair convention.

periods.activity_title: Deriving the Distance Formula from the Baudhayana-Pythagoras Theorem
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of the right triangle ADM used in the derivation of the distance formula (Section 1.4)

time_bands.activity: Pose the motivating problem: given two points in different quadrants, how do you find the straight-line distance between them? Students suggest approaches. Establish that a horizontal or vertical distance is simply the absolute difference of the matching coordinates — work one example on the board with two points that share a y-coordinate. Then ask: what if the two points share neither coordinate?

Derive the distance formula following Section 1.4: for points (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), construct the right triangle by drawing the horizontal leg of length |x₂ − x₁| and the vertical leg of length |y₂ − y₁|, then apply the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem to obtain d = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²). Name the triangle's vertices as the textbook does (A, D, M) and label each side. Students reproduce the derivation in their notebooks step by step.

Think-and-Reflect from Section 1.4 (first prompt): how do the horizontal and vertical shifts between two plotted points relate to the straight-line distance? Students articulate in one sentence that the legs of the right triangle ARE the coordinate differences, and the hypotenuse is the distance sought. Then pose the second prompt: after reflecting the triangle into negative-coordinate regions, do its side lengths change? Students reason that squaring the coordinate differences eliminates the sign — negative differences yield the same squared value — so the formula is sign-independent.

Consolidation check: teacher reads out two points, one with both coordinates positive and one with mixed signs, and students write the distance formula expression for that pair (without computing the square root) in their notebooks. This confirms that students can set up the formula correctly regardless of sign.

periods.teacher_notes: The derivation rests on the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem, which students should already know; if any student questions it, refer them to its geometric proof in their prior work rather than re-deriving it here. The most frequent algebraic error is writing (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² under the square root without squaring each difference — watch for students who write |x₂ − x₁| + |y₂ − y₁| instead. The reflection argument in the Think-and-Reflect (second prompt) is the conceptual heart: squaring removes the sign, so the formula works in every quadrant without modification.

periods.activity_title: Applying the Distance Formula: Triangle IZN and Quadrilateral ABCD

textbook_items_in_class.description: Plot point Z(5,-6), construct a right-angled triangle IZN, and find the lengths of its three sides.
Plot A(2,1), B(-1,2), C(-2,-1), D(1,-2); determine whether ABCD is a square, explain why, and find its area.

time_bands.activity: Students open to End of Chapter Q4 (p.12). Ask them to plot Z(5,−6) on graph paper first, then choose I and N to form a right-angled triangle with Z. Discuss briefly: what choices of I and N make the right angle easy to compute? The natural choices are I(5,0) and N(0,0) or I(5,0) and N(0,−6), which give axis-aligned legs.

Students complete End of Chapter Q4 (p.12): find the lengths of the two legs (by coordinate difference) and the hypotenuse (by the distance formula). They write each calculation step explicitly. Circulate; the common slip is using the distance formula for the leg lengths rather than simple coordinate subtraction — prompt students to see that a horizontal or vertical segment needs only subtraction.

Students work End of Chapter Q16 (p.14): plot A(2,1), B(−1,2), C(−2,−1), D(1,−2) on graph paper, compute all four side lengths using the distance formula, compute both diagonals, and determine whether ABCD is a square. The argument requires: four equal sides (all √10), equal diagonals (both 2√10), and right angles — students who establish the first two and compute the diagonal correctly have a complete justification. They state the area as side² = 10 square units.

Debrief: one student presents the ABCD square justification on the board. Teacher highlights that all four points lie one per quadrant — a detail that confirms the formula's sign-independence demonstrated in the derivation unit.

periods.teacher_notes: End of Chapter Q16 (p.14) is the richest application of the distance formula in the chapter: it draws on plotting across all four quadrants (from Section 1.3) and applies the formula repeatedly (Section 1.4). A frequent error is concluding ABCD is a square after finding only that the four sides are equal, without checking the diagonals or right angles — press students for a complete argument. For the area, students who compute base × height instead of side² often struggle because the square is tilted; direct them to area = side².

periods.activity_title: Real-World Distance Problems: Circles on a Screen and Consolidation

textbook_items_in_class.description: On an 800x600 pixel screen with origin at the bottom-left, given a radius-80 circle centred at A(100,150) and a radius-100 circle centred at B(250,230), determine whether any part of either circle lies outside the screen and whether the two circles intersect.
Sketch an 18 ft x 15 ft dining room running from point P to point A and mark its corner coordinates; place a 5x3 ft dining table at the centre of the room and give the coordinates of its feet.

time_bands.activity: Brief orientation to End of Chapter Q15 (p.14): the screen's coordinate system has the origin at the bottom-left and axes along the edges, so all points on the screen have non-negative coordinates. Ask students to state the coordinates of the screen's four corners before they begin the problem.

Students work End of Chapter Q15 (p.14) in two parts. Part (i): for each circle, compare centre coordinate ± radius against the screen bounds (0, 800) for x and (0, 600) for y — this is a reading of coordinates as perpendicular distances from the axes. Part (ii): compute the distance between A(100,150) and B(250,230) using the distance formula and compare it with 80 + 100 = 180. If d < 180 the circles intersect; students calculate d and state their conclusion with the comparison written out.

Students who finish early tackle Exercise Set 1.2 Q4 (p.8) — placing the dining table at the room's centre and giving corner coordinates — as consolidation of the coordinate-reading skills from Section 1.3. For the rest of the class, teacher leads a whole-class check of the circle-intersection calculation: one student writes d = √((250−100)² + (230−150)²) on the board and evaluates it step by step.

Closing synthesis: teacher poses one open question — 'What are the two main things coordinates let you do?' — and takes responses. Students should arrive at: (1) name any point's exact position, and (2) compute the distance between any two points. This closes the chapter's two principal ideas without reference to any other sitting.

periods.teacher_notes: End of Chapter Q15 (p.14) is the chapter's richest cross-context application, combining coordinate reading (Section 1.3) with the distance formula (Section 1.4). A common error in the circle-boundary check is testing only the centre's coordinates rather than centre ± radius; press students to check all four directions for each circle. The closing synthesis question is deliberately open-ended: students who articulate both functions of coordinates — location and distance — have reached the chapter's stated learning destination.

competency.competency_text: Specifying the location of a point and describing spatial relationships between points using coordinate geometry.

questions.question_text: A student claims: 'A coordinate system with only whole numbers and zero is perfectly sufficient to name any point on a flat plane — there is no need for negative numbers.' Using what you know about how the Cartesian plane is structured, write a detailed argument that either supports or refutes this claim. Your response must refer to at least one specific feature of the four-quadrant plane that depends on negative numbers.
look_for: Identifies that without negative numbers only Quadrant I is accessible — points to the left of or below the origin cannot be named.
States explicitly that the x-axis and y-axis extend in both directions, and the negative direction requires negative coordinate values.
Connects this to Brahmagupta's formalisation of zero and negative numbers as the structural precondition for the four-quadrant plane.
Refutes the student's claim with a concrete counter-example: names a point such as (−3, 2) and explains why it cannot be located in a non-negative system.
Concludes that only one-quarter of the infinite plane (Quadrant I and the positive parts of the axes) is reachable without negative numbers.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to begin may be prompted: 'Draw the axes and mark one point in Quadrant II — what sign must its x-coordinate have?' Students who complete the argument quickly may be challenged: 'Could you build a different kind of coordinate system using only non-negative numbers that still covers the whole plane? What would you have to change about the origin's position?'
ECR.lift_note: This item receives a Rule 6 reasoning-floor lift: the section's implied_lo was classified as Analysis, which maps to ECR directly. The lift records that without this item the assessment would contain no extended-reasoning task.

questions.question_text: Priya is making a scale plan of her rectangular bedroom, which is 12 ft long and 9 ft wide. She uses the scale 1 cm = 1 ft and places her diagram on plain paper without marking any origin or labels. She places a pin for the door hinge at the point that is 3 ft along the longer wall from one corner and 0 ft from the shorter wall. (a) Sketch Priya's room on squared paper at the given scale, marking the four corners and the door hinge. (b) Priya's friend looks at the same diagram and says the door hinge is '3 ft along and 0 ft up from the corner at the other end of the longer wall.' Explain, in one or two sentences, why both descriptions are correct and what this reveals about an informal grid without a fixed origin.
expected_elements: A correctly proportioned rectangle 12 cm × 9 cm on squared paper with four corners marked.
The door hinge marked at a point 3 cm from one corner along the longer (12 cm) wall and on that wall (0 cm from the shorter wall).

A written explanation that correctly identifies the ambiguity: without a fixed origin, the same physical point can be measured from different reference corners, producing different number pairs that are both accurate.
An implicit or explicit statement that fixing an origin and an ordered-pair convention removes the ambiguity.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find the sketch difficult may first mark just two corners and the door hinge on a number line before extending to a 2-D diagram. Students who complete part (b) quickly may be asked: 'How many different valid descriptions of the door hinge's position could be given if any of the four corners is allowed as a reference point? Could two of those descriptions produce the same number pair?'

questions.implied_lo_assessed: Students can determine the coordinates of a point in the Cartesian plane by applying the sign convention and the definition of x- and y-coordinates as perpendicular distances from the axes.
questions.section_context: Axes, origin, four quadrants, sign convention, and ordered-pair coordinates of points and figures

competency.competency_text: Specifying the location of a point and describing spatial relationships between points using coordinate geometry.

questions.question_text: A point T lies in the Cartesian plane. Its perpendicular distance from the y-axis is 4 units, and it is located to the left of the y-axis. Its perpendicular distance from the x-axis is 3 units, and it is located below the x-axis. What are the coordinates of T?

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student ignores the direction signs entirely and writes the two distances as positive coordinates, showing the sign convention for left/below has not been applied.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student applies the correct signs but transposes the two distances, placing the perpendicular distance from the x-axis first and the distance from the y-axis second — the classic x/y axis-confusion reversal.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student correctly signs the y-coordinate (below the x-axis is negative) but treats the x-coordinate as positive despite the point being to the left of the y-axis — partial application of the sign convention.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who hesitate may be encouraged to sketch a blank coordinate plane, mark the axes, and physically count four units to the left and three units down from the origin before reading off the coordinate pair. Students who answer quickly may be asked: 'For which coordinates (a, b) does swapping give the same point (b, a) = (a, b)?'

questions.question_text: Three corners of a rectangle are given as P(−6, 5), Q(2, 5), and R(2, −3). (a) Plot P, Q, and R on the coordinate plane. (b) Find the coordinates of the fourth corner S. (c) State which side of the rectangle is parallel to the x-axis and which is parallel to the y-axis, justifying each answer using the coordinates. Show all working.
questions.expected_answer: S = (−6, −3); PQ and SR are parallel to the x-axis (shared y-coordinate 5 and −3 respectively); QR and PS are parallel to the y-axis (shared x-coordinate 2 and −6 respectively).
questions.method_one_line: Opposite vertices of a rectangle share exactly one coordinate: S shares the x-coordinate of P and the y-coordinate of R, giving S(−6, −3); sides parallel to an axis are identified by the equality of the matching coordinate across both endpoints.

NUM.inclusivity: Students who are unsure how to find S may be prompted to sketch the three points and ask 'which corner is missing from the rectangle?' before identifying the shared coordinates. Students who finish quickly may be asked: 'If you shift the entire rectangle 3 units to the right, what are the new coordinates of all four corners? Which structural properties are preserved?'

competency.competency_text: Specifying the location of a point and describing spatial relationships between points using coordinate geometry.

questions.question_text: Points J(−3, 4) and K(5, −2) are marked in the Cartesian plane. (a) Plot J and K on the coordinate plane and draw the horizontal and vertical line segments that form the two legs of a right-angled triangle with JK as the hypotenuse. Label the third vertex of this triangle as L, and state its coordinates. (b) Find the lengths of the two legs JL and LK. (c) Use the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem to find the length JK, leaving your answer in surd form. Show all steps.
questions.expected_answer: L = (5, 4); JL = 8 units (horizontal leg, |5 − (−3)| = 8); LK = 6 units (vertical leg, |4 − (−2)| = 6); JK = √(8² + 6²) = √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10 units.
questions.method_one_line: Construct L at (x₂, y₁) = (5, 4) so that JL is horizontal and LK is vertical; compute each leg as a coordinate difference; apply the Baudhayana-Pythagoras theorem: JK = √(JL² + LK²).

NUM.inclusivity: Students who are unsure where to place L may be reminded that L must share the x-coordinate of one given point and the y-coordinate of the other, so that one leg is perfectly horizontal and one perfectly vertical. Students who complete the item quickly may be asked: 'Confirm your answer by computing JK directly using the distance formula d = √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²) and checking that you get the same result.'
